notes.definition: Atoms are very small, with a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m). Almost all of their mass is in the tiny nucleus, and the mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons.
explanation: Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm, which is 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m). The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom, about 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. To picture this, if a nucleus were the size of a pea in the centre of a football pitch, the atom would be about the size of the whole stadium. This is why most of an atom is empty space.

Almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus. The relative mass of a proton is 1 and the relative mass of a neutron is 1, while the relative mass of an electron is very small (about 1/1840, so it is usually ignored). Since the protons and neutrons are both in the nucleus, the nucleus contains almost all the mass even though it is a tiny fraction of the volume.

The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom is its mass number. Atoms can be represented using the mass number and atomic number, for example ²³₁₁Na. The top number is the mass number (23) and the bottom number is the atomic number (11). So a sodium-23 atom has 11 protons, 11 electrons and 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons. Remember: number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. These atoms are called isotopes of that element. Isotopes have the same number of protons (and so the same atomic number) but different mass numbers. For example, chlorine has two common isotopes: ³⁵₁₇Cl has 17 protons and 18 neutrons, while ³⁷₁₇Cl has 17 protons and 20 neutrons. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are also isotopes. Isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons, so they react in the same way.

You should be able to calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or an ion. The number of protons and neutrons is the same in an ion as in the atom; only the number of electrons changes. A positive ion has lost electrons and a negative ion has gained electrons. For ²⁷₁₃Al³⁺: protons = 13, neutrons = 27 − 13 = 14, electrons = 13 − 3 = 10. For ³²₁₆S²⁻: protons = 16, neutrons = 16, electrons = 16 + 2 = 18. Because electrons have so little mass, an ion has the same mass number as its atom.
keyFacts: Radius of an atom: about 0.1 nm = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.
Radius of a nucleus: less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius, about 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.
Almost all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.
Relative masses: proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small.
Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons.
Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
In ²³₁₁Na the top number (23) is the mass number and the bottom number (11) is the atomic number.
Isotopes: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Positive ions have fewer electrons than protons; negative ions have more electrons than protons.

keyTerms.definition: The distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outer edge of the atom, about 0.1 nm.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.
The number of protons in an atom.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The mass of a particle compared with the mass of a proton (1).
A unit of length equal to 1 × 10⁻⁹ m.
A way of writing very large or small numbers as A × 10ⁿ, where A is between 1 and 10, for example 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

workedExamples.title: Protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom
workedExamples.question: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in an atom of ³⁹₁₉K?

workedExamples.title: Particles in an ion
workedExamples.question: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in the ion ¹⁶₈O²⁻?
steps: The 2− charge means 2 extra electrons: electrons = 8 + 2 = 10.

workedExamples.title: Standard form and unit conversion
workedExamples.question: An atom has a radius of 0.15 nm. Write this in metres in standard form, and estimate the radius of its nucleus if it is 1/10 000 of the atom's radius.
workedExamples.answer: Atom radius = 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; nucleus radius ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.

workedExamples.title: Comparing sizes
workedExamples.question: The radius of an atom is 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and the radius of its nucleus is 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. How many times larger is the atom?
steps: Divide the atom radius by the nucleus radius: (1 × 10⁻¹⁰) ÷ (1 × 10⁻¹⁴).
When dividing powers of ten, subtract the indices: −10 − (−14) = 4.
workedExamples.answer: The atom's radius is 10 000 times larger than the nucleus's radius.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the mass number is the number of neutrons.
misconceptions.right: In fact the mass number is protons plus neutrons. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think isotopes are different elements.
misconceptions.right: In fact isotopes are atoms of the same element: same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think forming an ion changes the number of protons.
misconceptions.right: In fact only electrons are gained or lost. The protons and neutrons, and so the mass number, stay the same.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think electrons add significantly to the mass of an atom.
misconceptions.right: In fact an electron's relative mass is very small (about 1/1840 of a proton), so almost all the mass is in the nucleus.

realWorld: Carbon-14, a radioactive isotope of carbon, is used in radiocarbon dating of archaeological remains.
Scanning tunnelling microscopes can image individual atoms because they can resolve distances of around 0.1 nm.
Hospitals use isotopes such as iodine-131 and technetium-99m, which behave chemically like other isotopes of the same element, to diagnose and treat disease.
examTips: In nuclide notation the bigger number is always the mass number; use it minus the smaller number to get neutrons.
For ions, change only the electrons: subtract for positive charges, add for negative charges.
When converting nm to m, multiply by 10⁻⁹ and then make sure the answer is in proper standard form (first number between 1 and 10).
When dividing numbers in standard form, divide the front numbers and subtract the powers.
summary: Atoms have a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).
The nucleus radius is less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius.
Almost all the mass is in the nucleus: protons and neutrons have relative mass 1, electrons very small.
Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Ions have the same protons and neutrons as the atom but a different number of electrons.

questions.question: What is the approximate radius of an atom?
questions.explanation: Atoms have a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m). 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m is roughly the radius of a nucleus.

questions.question: Where is almost all of the mass of an atom found?
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons (relative mass 1 each) are in the nucleus. Electrons have very little mass.

questions.question: What is the relative mass of a neutron?
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1. The electron's mass is very small. 0 is the neutron's charge, not its mass.

questions.question: The mass number of an atom is the:
markScheme: 1 mark: number of protons plus neutrons
questions.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons, the particles in the nucleus that have significant mass.

questions.question: Which statement describes isotopes?
options: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of protons
Atoms with more electrons than protons
markScheme: 1 mark: atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
questions.explanation: Isotopes share the same number of protons but have different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers. Atoms with more electrons than protons are negative ions.

questions.question: Which is 0.1 nm written in metres in standard form?
questions.explanation: 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m, so 0.1 nm = 0.1 × 10⁻⁹ m = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. 1 × 10⁻⁹ m is 1 nm, ten times too big.

questions.question: How does the radius of a nucleus compare with the radius of the whole atom?
options: It is about half the radius of the atom
It is about 1/100 of the radius of the atom
It is the same as the radius of the atom
It is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom
markScheme: 1 mark: less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom
questions.explanation: The nucleus is tiny: about 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m compared with 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m for the atom.

questions.question: Which pair of atoms are isotopes of the same element?
questions.explanation: Both carbon atoms have 6 protons but different mass numbers. ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N have the same mass number but different numbers of protons, so they are different elements.

questions.question: An atom of oxygen-18 is represented as ¹⁸₈O. Which row is correct for this atom?
questions.explanation: Protons = 8; neutrons = 18 − 8 = 10; electrons in an atom = protons = 8. 18 is the mass number, not the number of neutrons.

questions.question: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in the calcium ion ⁴⁰₂₀Ca²⁺?
questions.explanation: A 2+ ion has lost 2 electrons: 20 − 2 = 18. Protons and neutrons do not change. Adding 2 electrons would give a 2− ion.

questions.question: How many neutrons are there in an atom of ²³₁₁Na?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.

questions.question: An atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. What is its mass number?
questions.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35. This is chlorine-35.

questions.question: How many neutrons are there in an atom of ³⁷₁₇Cl?
questions.explanation: 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons.

questions.question: How many electrons are there in the aluminium ion ²⁷₁₃Al³⁺?
questions.explanation: The atom has 13 electrons. A 3+ ion has lost 3 electrons: 13 − 3 = 10.

questions.question: How many electrons are there in the sulfide ion ³²₁₆S²⁻?
questions.explanation: The atom has 16 electrons. A 2− ion has gained 2 electrons: 16 + 2 = 18.

questions.question: The radius of an atom is 0.1 nm. Give this radius in metres. (1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m)
questions.explanation: 0.1 × 10⁻⁹ m = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Moving the decimal point one place right makes the power one more negative.

questions.question:
The radius of an atom is 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The radius of its nucleus is 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.
Calculate how many times larger the radius of the atom is than the radius of the nucleus.
questions.explanation: Divide and subtract the powers: 10⁻¹⁰⁻⁽⁻¹⁴⁾ = 10⁴ = 10 000.

questions.question: A gold atom has a radius of 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Give this radius in nanometres. (1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m)
questions.explanation: Divide by 1 × 10⁻⁹: 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 10⁻⁹ = 1.44 × 10⁻¹ = 0.144 nm. An answer of 1.44 nm comes from forgetting that 10⁻¹⁰ is smaller than 10⁻⁹.

questions.question:
An atom has a radius of 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Its nucleus has a radius 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom.
Calculate the radius of the nucleus. Give your answer in metres in standard form.
questions.explanation: Dividing by 10⁴ subtracts 4 from the power: 10⁻¹⁰ becomes 10⁻¹⁴.

questions.question:
A teacher builds a scale model of an atom. The nucleus is a bead of radius 1 cm. The radius of a real atom is 10 000 times the radius of its nucleus.
Calculate the radius the model atom would need, in metres.
questions.explanation: 10 000 cm is 100 m, because there are 100 cm in 1 m. This shows how much empty space there is in an atom.

questions.question: State what is meant by the mass number of an atom.
acceptedAnswers: total number of particles in the nucleus
markScheme: 1 mark: the total number of protons and neutrons (in the nucleus)
questions.explanation: Electrons are not counted because their mass is very small.

questions.question: Define the term isotopes.
markScheme: 1 mark: atoms of the same element / with the same number of protons
1 mark: with different numbers of neutrons
questions.explanation: Both parts are needed. Saying different mass numbers is acceptable for the second mark only if same element is also stated.

questions.question: State the relative mass of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
questions.explanation: The electron's mass is so small that it is usually ignored when working out mass numbers.

questions.question: Explain why almost all the mass of an atom is in its nucleus.
markScheme: 1 mark: protons and neutrons (each relative mass 1) are in the nucleus
1 mark: electrons, outside the nucleus, have a very small mass
questions.explanation: The heavy particles are concentrated in the nucleus even though it is a tiny part of the atom's volume.

questions.question: Chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl. Compare the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms of these two isotopes.
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine-35 has 18 neutrons and chlorine-37 has 20 neutrons
questions.explanation: Isotopes differ only in the number of neutrons: 35 − 17 = 18 and 37 − 17 = 20.

questions.question: An atom has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Write the symbol for this atom showing its mass number and atomic number, and name the element.
markScheme: 1 mark: ¹⁴₆C (mass number 14 at top, atomic number 6 at bottom)
questions.explanation: Mass number = 6 + 8 = 14. Atomic number 6 is carbon, so this is carbon-14.

questions.question: Argon-40 is ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and calcium-40 is ⁴⁰₂₀Ca. Explain why these two atoms are not isotopes, even though they have the same mass number.
acceptedAnswers: isotopes must be the same element
markScheme: 1 mark: they have different numbers of protons (18 and 20) / different atomic numbers, so they are different elements
1 mark: isotopes must be atoms of the same element (same protons) with different numbers of neutrons
questions.explanation: Having the same mass number does not make atoms isotopes. Ar-40 has 22 neutrons and Ca-40 has 20 neutrons, but the key point is the different numbers of protons.

questions.question: A sodium atom, ²³₁₁Na, loses one electron to form a sodium ion, Na⁺. Explain why the mass number of the ion is still 23.
acceptedAnswers: mass number counts protons and neutrons
markScheme: 1 mark: the mass number counts protons and neutrons, which do not change when an ion forms
1 mark: only an electron is lost, and electrons have a very small (negligible) mass
questions.explanation: Ion formation only changes the electrons, which are not included in the mass number.

questions.question:
The radius of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and the radius of its nucleus is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.
Compare the size and mass of the nucleus with the size and mass of the whole atom, and explain what this tells us about the structure of an atom.
markScheme: Indicative content: the atom's radius is about 10 000 times the radius of the nucleus (nucleus less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius); the nucleus is a tiny part of the volume; but almost all the mass is in the nucleus because protons and neutrons (relative mass 1) are there; electrons have very small mass and are outside the nucleus; so most of the atom is empty space, with a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear comparison of size and mass using the data, with a correct conclusion about empty space and a dense nucleus.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as the nucleus is smaller or contains the mass.
questions.explanation: The numbers show the nucleus is 10 000 times smaller in radius, yet it contains nearly all the mass.

questions.question:
Chlorine exists as two isotopes, ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl. A chlorine atom can gain one electron to form a chloride ion, Cl⁻.
Describe the structure of the atoms of both isotopes and of a ³⁵Cl⁻ ion. Include the numbers and locations of the subatomic particles, their relative masses, and explain which features are the same and which are different.
markScheme: Indicative content: both isotopes have 17 protons in the nucleus (same atomic number, same element); chlorine-35 has 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons and chlorine-37 has 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons; both atoms have 17 electrons in shells around the nucleus; protons and neutrons have relative mass 1, electrons very small, so almost all mass is in the nucleus and mass numbers are 35 and 37; the ³⁵Cl⁻ ion has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons (one extra electron); the ion has the same mass number (35) because electrons have negligible mass; same: protons; different between isotopes: neutrons and mass; different between atom and ion: electrons and charge.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct numbers of all particles for both isotopes and the ion, with locations, relative masses and a clear explanation of what is the same and what differs.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): mostly correct numbers for the isotopes and some correct comment on the ion or on relative masses.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct numbers or simple statements, for example that isotopes have different neutrons.
questions.explanation: This brings together mass number, isotopes and ions. The ion changes only the electrons, while the isotopes differ only in neutrons.
